items.question: A grocery retailer is launching Claude-written product descriptions on its storefront. The team wants the first exposure limited to a cohort it can reason about, held stable per shopper, and reversible within seconds if merchandising objects. Which flag design fits?

options.A: A build-time constant compiled into the release binary, flipped by cutting and shipping a new build to the affected storefront regions.
options.B: A server-side flag evaluated per request, made stable per shopper by a bucketing hash, defaulting to off and changeable without a deploy.
options.C: A client-side flag written to local storage on first app launch, so a shopper keeps the same assignment across sessions and devices.
options.D: An environment variable read once at process start, toggled by rolling the fleet with a new value set in the deployment manifest.

items.question: A quant research desk must be able to justify any Claude-generated commentary attached to a trade, years after execution. An engineer proposes setting temperature to 0 and storing only the input text, arguing that the commentary is then a pure function of that input and can be regenerated on demand. Which assessment is correct?

options.A: Correct: greedy decoding makes the output a deterministic function of the prompt, so the input text plus the request timestamp is a sufficient audit record for the desk.
options.B: Wrong parameter: determinism comes from pinning top_p and top_k rather than temperature, so those are the values the desk must fix and record alongside each input.
options.C: Incomplete: temperature 0 removes sampling variance but not serving-side or model-version variance, so the stored output itself must be the audit record.
options.D: Wrong approach: audit reproducibility is only achievable by self-hosting a pinned open-weights model, because no hosted service can offer identical regeneration across years.

items.question: In a prompt library versioned alongside application code and consumed by several services, which change should be released as breaking rather than as a patch?

options.A: Adding a new required template variable, so an existing caller's render either fails outright or silently omits the context the instruction now assumes.
options.B: Rewording an instruction for clarity while the set of template variables and the rendered output schema both stay identical for every caller.
options.C: Appending two further few-shot examples to an existing example block, after the eval suite showed a measurable improvement on a known weak case.
options.D: Raising the documented maximum input length for the template after testing confirmed that longer inputs still render and grade correctly.

items.question: A fintech captures sampled production requests into an eval fixture corpus so that prompt changes can be regression-tested against real traffic. Six months in, a security review finds fixtures containing live API tokens that customers had pasted into support chats, and the fixture repository is readable by all 200 engineers. Which remediation addresses the systemic problem rather than this instance of it?

options.A: Rotate every token discovered in the corpus, notify the affected customers, and record the exposure window in the incident register for the regulator.
options.B: Restrict the fixture repository to the four engineers who maintain the eval suite, and require an access request with justification for anyone else.
options.C: Add a scheduled scanner over the fixture repository that raises a ticket to the security team whenever a stored value matches a known credential pattern.
options.D: Run secret detection and redaction at the capture boundary, so a value that looks like a credential is never written into the fixture store in the first place.

items.question: A national newspaper's Claude-based headline-suggestion tool has for 40 minutes been producing suggestions that embed a competitor's brand name; two have already reached publication. The feature sits behind a server-side percentage flag currently set to 100%. Its prompt was updated 50 minutes ago; reverting that commit and completing a deploy takes about 12 minutes. The editor-in-chief has joined the incident call. What should the incident commander do first?

options.A: Revert the prompt commit and start the deploy, since the change 50 minutes ago is the obvious cause and the fix should go in at the root.
options.B: Pull a sample of the last 40 minutes of suggestions to quantify how many contain the brand name, so the response is proportionate to the actual scope.
options.C: Set the flag to 0% to stop new suggestions immediately, then work the prompt change and the two published headlines as parallel tracks.
options.D: Ship a post-generation filter that blocks competitor brand names in suggestions, which fixes this class of failure rather than just this occurrence.

items.question: A platform team is choosing the primary unit in which it reports Claude spend back to the product teams that consume it. Which unit best supports a budget conversation with those teams?

options.A: Cost per completed business task, such as per resolved support ticket or per document processed end to end.
options.B: Cost per million tokens, since that is the unit the provider invoices in and it therefore needs no translation or assumptions.
options.C: Cost per API request, since each request maps one to one onto a line already present in the gateway's access log.
options.D: Cost per engineer per month, since headcount is the dimension the finance system already uses to allocate every other budget.

items.question: A manufacturing group runs Claude-based defect-report triage at roughly 900,000 requests a month. Capturing every trace with rendered prompts would cost more than the inference itself, so the platform team samples 1% of traces at the head. Quality engineers report the same frustration every time: whenever a customer-reported bad triage is investigated, that specific trace was not among the sampled ones. Which sampling change best fits this workload?

options.A: Raise head sampling from 1% to 10%: a missing trace becomes ten times less likely, at one tenth of the cost of capturing every trace in full.
options.B: Keep head sampling at 1% but extend retention on the sampled traces from 90 days to seven years, so that any historical investigation always has some material to work from.
options.C: Adopt tail-based sampling: decide after the request completes, keeping traces that errored, ran long, or were flagged by a quality signal, plus a small random baseline.
options.D: Stop capturing traces and rely on the application's structured logs, which already record a line for the request and the response of every call.

items.question: For an AI-powered feature, why is an incident in which the feature returns confident but wrong output often rated more severe than an outage of the same duration?

options.A: An outage announces itself and users stop relying on the feature, whereas wrong output is consumed as correct and its effects spread downstream.
options.B: Wrong output consumes more tokens per request than a failed call does, so financial impact accumulates faster across the incident window.
options.C: Availability is covered by the platform's SLO while output quality usually has none, so the wrong-output case has no owner on the on-call rota.
options.D: Wrong output normally indicates a provider-side model regression the team cannot fix, whereas an outage is generally inside the team's own control.

items.question: A retail bank's AI platform team loses about three weeks per new hire before that engineer can safely make a change. A retrospective identifies two dominant blockers: newcomers cannot tell which prompt an observed production behaviour came from, and they cannot run the system locally because every path requires production credentials. The team has budget for two investments this quarter. Which TWO address those blockers directly? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Publish a weekly digest of production quality metrics to the team channel so that newcomers gradually absorb how the system behaves over time.
options.B: Stamp the prompt template identifier and version onto every stored response record, so any observed output resolves to a specific file and commit.
options.C: Introduce a mandatory architecture review for any change that touches more than one prompt template in the shared library.
options.D: Grant every new hire read-only production database access on day one so they can inspect real records while learning the domain model.
options.E: Ship a recorded-fixture mode that replays captured tool results and stored model responses, letting the whole chain run locally with no live dependency.

items.question: A university's research-support assistant runs on a departmental budget that cannot be exceeded without a fresh approval from the faculty finance committee. Usage is bursty, spiking hard during assessment weeks. Today the only control is an email alert at 80% of the monthly budget. Twice this year the department has blown past the cap in the hours between the alert firing and someone reading it. What control should be added?

options.A: Lower the alert threshold from 80% to 60% of budget, giving whoever is on duty considerably more headroom between the first warning and the cap.
options.B: Move the department onto an annual rather than a monthly budget, so a single assessment-week spike is absorbed by the quieter months either side of it.
options.C: Charge any overage to the central platform budget and reconcile with the department quarterly, so no research request is ever blocked mid-term.
options.D: Enforce the ceiling at the gateway: degrade to the cheaper tier as spend nears the limit, then refuse non-essential traffic, with a documented override path.

items.question: What does running a new Claude-based component in shadow mode give a team that a 1% canary does not?

options.A: It guarantees the new component causes no side effects, because shadow traffic is read-only by construction and cannot invoke tools that write.
options.B: Every production request exercises the new component, so quality is measured across the full traffic distribution while no user sees its output.
options.C: It produces latency comparisons faster, because shadow requests skip the network overhead that a real client connection imposes on the measurement.
options.D: It lets real users give feedback on the new component's output before promotion, which a small canary cohort cannot gather at useful volume.

items.question: A payments processor asks Claude to return a JSON object listing unmatched transactions for reconciliation. Parse failures are negligible on ordinary days but reach 4% during end-of-month peaks, when unmatched lists are at their longest. Replaying a failing request reproduces the failure exactly. The team's first instinct is to wrap the parser in a JSON-repair library and move on. What is the more likely root cause to establish first?

options.A: Concurrency at peak is causing the client to interleave two streamed responses into a single buffer, corrupting the JSON before it reaches the parser.
options.B: Schema adherence degrades as inputs grow longer, so the prompt needs additional few-shot examples demonstrating the exact JSON shape required.
options.C: The response is hitting the configured maximum output tokens and stopping mid-object; the stop reason on the failing calls will say so directly.
options.D: An autoscaling configuration is raising temperature at peak, making the model more likely to deviate from the requested schema under load.

items.question: A user of a legal-research assistant reports that yesterday the tool cited a case that does not exist. They supply a screenshot with a visible timestamp and their account identifier. The team samples traces at 2% and this request was not among them; rendered prompts are not logged at all. The retrieval index is snapshotted nightly and the prompt library is versioned in the repository. What is the most useful next step?

options.A: Determine whether the cited case exists in the retrieval index as it stood yesterday, and what has changed in the prompt or index since.
options.B: Re-run the user's query against the current system and compare the answer with the screenshot, treating a mismatch as evidence the issue has resolved itself.
options.C: Raise trace sampling to 100% for the assistant and wait for the failure to recur, so that a complete record exists the next time it happens.
options.D: Open a provider support ticket attaching the screenshot as evidence of a hallucination, and pause the feature until the provider responds.

items.question: An engineer discovers that a production access token has been interpolated into a Claude prompt and sent with every request for the past week. What is the correct response?

options.A: Remove the interpolation in the next release and watch the token for anomalous use, rotating it only if suspicious activity actually appears in the logs.
options.B: Treat the token as compromised: rotate it now, remove the interpolation, and purge it from stored prompts, traces and captured eval fixtures.
options.C: Confirm the requests fell under a zero-retention arrangement with the provider, and rotate the token only if that arrangement turns out not to cover them.
options.D: Rotate the token but leave the stored prompts and traces untouched, since rotation renders the historical copies harmless from that point onward.

items.question: Six months after rolling out AI coding assistance, a logistics company's engineering leadership wants an honest read on whether it is helping. Adoption is uneven and self-selected: about 40% of engineers use it daily, 35% weekly, and 25% not at all. Leadership has asked for a number it can defend to the CFO. Which measurement design gives the most defensible answer?

options.A: Compare the same teams' delivery metrics before and after rollout and attribute the difference to the tool, since the teams and the codebase are held constant.
options.B: Withdraw the tool from a randomly chosen half of engineers for a quarter and compare completed story points between the two groups.
options.C: Ask every engineer to self-report hours saved per week, multiply by loaded cost, and publish the resulting annualised saving figure.
options.D: Compare change lead time and change failure rate between heavy and non-users, report the result as correlational, and pair it with a developer experience survey.

items.question: Two teams at a travel company consume the same itinerary-summary prompt from a shared library. Four months ago Team A needed a stricter tone for corporate clients and copied the template into its own repository, because the shared version had no way to express that. Since then the shared template has received three accuracy fixes; Team A's fork has none, and its measured accuracy has drifted below the shared version's. Team A maintains the fork was necessary. What is the right structural response?

options.A: Keep the fork but add a scheduled job that opens a pull request against it whenever the upstream template changes, so Team A can review and merge each fix.
options.B: Move both teams onto fully independent templates and accept the duplication as the ordinary cost of team autonomy on a shared platform.
options.C: Parameterise the shared template so tone is an explicit input, then delete the fork once Team A's cases pass the shared eval suite.
options.D: Forbid forking shared prompts as policy, revert Team A to the shared version, and route any remaining tone concerns to the platform team's backlog.

items.question: An organisation with a mature conventional secrets programme is hardening secret handling around its AI development workflow. Which TWO practices address exposure paths that its existing programme does not already cover? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Redacting credential-shaped strings from tool results before those results are appended to the model's context on the next turn.
options.B: Holding service credentials in a managed secrets manager rather than in environment files committed alongside application code.
options.C: Running a pre-commit secret scanner over every push so that credential patterns are caught before they enter version history.
options.D: Scrubbing captured production prompts before they are stored as eval fixtures or shared with a vendor during a debugging engagement.
options.E: Enforcing short-lived, automatically rotated credentials for all service-to-service calls so that any leaked value expires quickly.

items.question: A telehealth provider's clinical-note summarisation pipeline runs synchronously to an ingest API, hands off to a message queue, then to a worker that makes two Claude calls, then to a webhook callback. Traces show a complete span tree up to the enqueue and an entirely separate, unparented trace beginning at the worker. Investigating a bad summary currently means matching the two by timestamp and patient reference by hand. What is the fix?

options.A: Have the worker log the queue message identifier on every span, so an investigator can join the producer and consumer traces on that field afterwards.
options.B: Propagate the trace context inside the message envelope and start the worker's spans as children of the producing span.
options.C: Replace the queue with a synchronous call so the request never crosses a boundary that breaks the trace in the first place.
options.D: Increase the sampling rate on the worker service so more of its traces are retained and a matching one is likelier to exist when needed.

items.question: An insurer's claims-summarisation service normally costs about £9,000 a month. Last month it cost £31,000 while request volume rose only 6%. Two changes shipped in that window: conversation history sent with each call was extended from 3 turns to 10, and a retry policy was added that retries any non-2xx response up to five times. The team has per-request token counts, full trace data and deploy history. Which single analysis most quickly attributes the spike?

options.A: Compute cost per logical request before and after the deploy, which quantifies the jump precisely and confirms that volume growth is not responsible.
options.B: Sample 50 traces from the expensive month and read their rendered prompts to see how long the conversation histories have actually become in practice.
options.C: Disable the retry policy for a week and observe whether spend returns towards baseline, isolating that change by removal under real traffic.
options.D: Compare mean input tokens per successful request across the deploy boundary, and separately count total attempts per logical request.

items.question: In the progressive rollout of an AI feature, what is the purpose of keeping a small holdback group on the previous behaviour after the feature reaches full rollout?

options.A: It provides a pool of users who can be switched back onto the feature instantly if it fails elsewhere, which shortens the overall time needed to roll back.
options.B: It lowers total inference cost by permanently leaving a defined slice of traffic on the cheaper legacy path rather than routing it through the model-backed one.
options.C: It preserves a comparison population, so post-launch quality and business-metric claims can still be tested against the previous behaviour.
options.D: It satisfies an obligation to obtain explicit consent from a sample of users before anyone is exposed to AI-generated content.

items.question: Six months after a 60-person games studio rolled out AI coding assistance, pull requests opened per week are up 45%, median pull-request size is up 30%, and cycle time from open to merge has risen 20%. Defect escape rate is unchanged. Leadership reads the first figure as a win and wants to expand the licence. What is the most plausible reading of the three figures together, and what follows from it?

options.A: The constraint has moved from writing code to reviewing it; measure and staff review capacity before treating the pull-request increase as delivered throughput.
options.B: The assistance is producing weaker code, so every AI-assisted change should be required to carry a second reviewer before it can be merged.
options.C: Cycle time is a lagging indicator that normalises as teams adjust to a new way of working; hold the rollout where it is and re-measure once two further quarters of data exist.
options.D: Engineers are batching more work into each change; impose a maximum pull-request size to bring cycle time back to its previous level.

items.question: An agriculture-technology firm runs a Claude agent that fails roughly once in 200 production runs by oscillating between two tools until it exhausts its step limit. Engineers have run thousands of staging executions and cannot reproduce it once. Which THREE differences between the environments are the most likely candidates to investigate first? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Staging runs against a small curated tool-result corpus, so the agent never meets the ambiguous, conflicting or empty results production returns.
options.B: Staging carries far lower concurrency, so each step completes with lower latency than the same step does in production.
options.C: Staging resolves a floating model alias while production pins a specific version, so the two environments are not running the same model.
options.D: Staging logs at DEBUG level while production logs at INFO, so the oscillation is only visible in one of the two environments.
options.E: Staging conversations are short, so the agent never reaches the context length at which earlier instructions begin to lose salience.

items.question: A shared gateway records total input tokens and total output tokens for every request, and finance uses those two figures to charge teams back. The platform team then enables prompt caching on the largest system prompts. Why do the recorded figures stop mapping to actual cost?

options.A: Caching removes tokens from the request entirely before transmission, so the gateway's recorded input count materially understates what the provider actually processed for the call.
options.B: Cache reads and cache writes are billed at different rates from ordinary input tokens, so one undifferentiated input total no longer corresponds to one cost.
options.C: Cache hits are served from a client-side store and never reach the gateway, so those requests are absent from the access log altogether.
options.D: Cached prefixes expire on a timer, so an identical recorded token count corresponds to a different cost depending on the time of day the call was made.

items.question: A logistics marketplace is at the 25% stage of rolling out AI-generated shipment descriptions. The promotion gate requires the model-graded quality score on sampled outputs to be no more than 2 points below the human-written baseline. The current reading from 120 sampled outputs is 1.8 points below baseline, with a 95% confidence interval running from 0.4 to 3.2 points below. The stage is stable on all operational signals and the team wants a decision today. What is the appropriate next step?

options.A: Promote to 100%: the point estimate satisfies the gate and the interval is symmetric around it, so the expected outcome is a pass.
options.B: Roll back to 5%, because part of the interval exceeds the threshold and a quality gate should fail closed whenever it is uncertain.
options.C: Hold at 25% and keep sampling until the interval sits wholly inside or wholly outside the 2-point threshold.
options.D: Relax the gate to 3 points for this rollout, since grader variance makes a 2-point threshold impractical at a sample size this small.

items.question: A broadcaster's live-captioning summariser began producing noticeably shorter, less specific summaries about ten days ago. The repository shows no change to the prompt in six weeks. The system prompt is loaded at container start from a configuration service that any engineer can edit through a web console, and that console keeps no change history. What should the team do?

options.A: Diff the prompt as actually served against the repository copy, then move the prompt into the deployed artefact so the two cannot diverge again.
options.B: Alert on mean summary length, so that the next regression of this kind surfaces within hours instead of after ten days of degraded captions.
options.C: Roll the whole fleet so every container reloads the configuration service's current value and all instances are demonstrably serving the same prompt.
options.D: Raise the summariser to a higher model tier until the cause of the shortening is understood, then step back down once the investigation concludes.

items.question: A new engineer needs to understand what a production prompt template is actually supposed to achieve before changing it. Which artefact conveys that most reliably?

options.A: The inline comments in the template file, written by whichever engineer most recently edited it.
options.B: The commit history of the template, which shows every change along with the reasoning captured in each message.
options.C: The eval set bound to the template, whose cases and expected outputs define the behaviour the prompt must produce.
options.D: The architecture diagram for the service, which shows where the template sits in the chain, what feeds into it, and which downstream component consumes its output.

items.question: A B2B expense-management SaaS runs Claude-based receipt categorisation for 400 tenants on one shared deployment. One large tenant reports that categorisation accuracy collapsed last Tuesday. Platform-wide accuracy over the same period is flat, no deploy shipped that day, and the tenant's request volume is normal. Traces with rendered prompts are retained for every tenant. What is the most productive first line of inquiry?

options.A: Ask the tenant for ten miscategorised receipts and re-run them through the current system to see whether the failures reproduce today.
options.B: Check whether this tenant resolves to a different model version or prompt variant, since large enterprise customers are frequently pinned to their own deployment configuration.
options.C: Raise trace sampling for this tenant and wait for further failures to accumulate into a set large enough to analyse statistically.
options.D: Diff this tenant's scoped inputs — their category taxonomy, custom rules and merchant list — across Monday and Tuesday, since a tenant-scoped effect implies a tenant-scoped cause.

items.question: A team is writing the review checklist for pull requests that change a prompt template in a shared library. Reviewers already read the diff carefully for clarity, tone and instruction conflicts. Which TWO additional checks catch failure modes that reading the diff cannot surface? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: An eval report attached to the pull request comparing golden-set scores before and after the change.
options.B: That the diff introduces no trailing whitespace or inconsistent indentation inside the template body.
options.C: That the commit message explains the motivation in terms a future reader unfamiliar with the ticket will understand.
options.D: The template rendered against a representative variable set, since the diff shows the source but not what the model receives.
options.E: That every service consuming the shared template has had its product owner sign off on the change before it merges.

items.question: An engineering director at a payments company proposes a team OKR: by year end, 50% of merged lines of code should be AI-generated. The intent is to accelerate adoption of an assistant the company has already paid for. A principal engineer is asked to comment before the OKR is published to the organisation. What is the most substantive objection?

options.A: Attribution is unreliable: once an engineer edits a suggestion, the line is no longer cleanly assignable to the assistant or to the person who reshaped it.
options.B: Targeting a share of AI-generated code rewards routing work through the assistant regardless of fit, and it is satisfiable without delivery improving at all.
options.C: Fifty percent is an arbitrary figure; a baseline should be measured first and the target then set as a relative improvement over that measured baseline.
options.D: The target belongs at individual rather than team level, so that adoption gaps between engineers become visible and can be addressed through coaching.

items.question: An eval suite runs on every pull request in CI, calling the live provider API with an organisation-wide key stored as a CI secret. Which change most reduces the blast radius if that secret leaks?

options.A: Rotate the CI secret monthly and record each rotation in the change log so auditors can confirm the cadence is being maintained.
options.B: Move the key into the organisation's secrets manager and have the CI job fetch it at start rather than holding it as a pipeline variable.
options.C: Restrict the workflow so it does not execute on pull requests raised from forks, where untrusted code could read the environment.
options.D: Issue CI its own key on a separate account with its own spend cap, and never share the production key with the pipeline at all.

items.question: A retail energy platform instrumented its Claude chain with OpenTelemetry. Within a month the tracing bill exceeded the inference bill. Investigation finds three things: spans carry the full user question plus one attribute per retrieved document id; a per-request unique key is used as a tag on metrics; and each service samples independently at 20%, so most stored traces are partial. The team must cut tracing cost while keeping the ability to investigate a specific bad output. Which THREE changes achieve that? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Move the user question and the retrieved document list off the span into a payload store, leaving a reference identifier on the span.
options.B: Remove the per-request unique key from metric tags, keeping it as a span attribute where high cardinality is expected and priced differently.
options.C: Reduce span retention from 30 days to 7 days across every service so the stored volume falls immediately.
options.D: Drop the tracing vendor and emit spans as structured application log lines instead, parsing them into a tree when an investigation needs one.
options.E: Make the sampling decision once at the edge and propagate it, so a trace is either kept whole or not kept at all.

items.question: A public transport authority ships a Claude-based disruption-notice writer behind a single flag that both enables the feature and selects which model version serves it. Six weeks later the team wants to move to a newer model version, and operations has asked that any problem with the move be reversible without taking the notice writer offline. What change should the team make first?

options.A: Split the two decisions into independent flags, so the model version can be rolled forward or back while the feature stays enabled.
options.B: Pin the flag to the new version in staging only and promote to production once staging has run clean for a full week under synthetic load.
options.C: Create a new flag for each model version and retire the previous flag after cutover, so each version's exposure is independently controllable.
options.D: Remove the flag and control the model version through the deployment artefact, since a version change is a code change and belongs in the release process.

items.question: A team's outputs changed noticeably overnight with no deploy, no prompt edit and no change to input data. Their client requests the model by a floating alias rather than a pinned version. What should be established first?

options.A: Whether an environment change on the serving hosts altered the sampling temperature or the top_p value that the client attaches to each outgoing request.
options.B: Which concrete model version the alias resolved to before and after the shift, using the version recorded on each response.
options.C: Whether the provider's status page reports degradation in the region the service routes its requests into.
options.D: Whether the prompt cache expired overnight, so the prefix was reprocessed and the output differs as a result.

items.question: A media company has eleven teams each building Claude-backed features independently. Engineers moving between teams find that no two services are instrumented, configured or evaluated the same way, and each internal move costs weeks of ramp. The platform team has capacity for one initiative this half. Which produces the most durable reduction in that cost?

options.A: Publish a standards document defining required instrumentation, prompt layout and eval conventions, then audit each team against it quarterly and track exceptions.
options.B: Run a monthly cross-team guild where engineers walk through how their service is structured, building shared familiarity across the eleven teams over time.
options.C: Ship a service template with tracing, prompt loading, eval wiring and cost tagging already in place, and migrate existing services onto it incrementally.
options.D: Centralise all eleven services under the platform team so that a single group owns the conventions and can apply them uniformly across the estate.

items.question: A platform team publishes a monthly Claude spend report to eight consuming teams. It shows each team's total spend and the month-on-month change, and in six months no team has changed anything in response to it. The platform team wants the report to drive action rather than acknowledgement. Which THREE additions would most plausibly achieve that? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: A league table ordering the eight teams by absolute spend, so the heaviest consumers appear at the top of the first page.
options.B: Cost per unit of business work for each team, so a team can see whether its spend per outcome is rising or falling.
options.C: A breakdown by feature or endpoint within each team, so spend attaches to something the team can actually change.
options.D: The provider's full rate card reproduced as an appendix, so teams can verify the platform team's arithmetic themselves.
options.E: Each team's cache hit rate and mean input tokens per request, the two levers most directly under the team's own control.

items.question: At 09:40 a children's-education platform receives a support ticket: a Claude-generated lesson summary shown to one class contained an inappropriate analogy, with a clear screenshot. Summaries are generated when a lesson is opened and cached for 24 hours, so that class can re-open the same text. The feature is enabled for 4,000 schools mid-term, no second instance has been reported, and the platform's incident policy requires action proportionate to observed harm. What should the on-call engineer do first?

options.A: Add the offending phrasing to the output blocklist and ship it, which stops that specific content being produced or served again anywhere.
options.B: Pull the trace for that lesson and establish whether the source material contained the analogy, before taking any action that affects other schools.
options.C: Disable the feature for all 4,000 schools until the cause is known, because the affected population is children and the content policy is strict.
options.D: Purge the cached summary so the class cannot re-open it, then investigate the trace while the feature continues serving other schools.

items.question: A logistics firm's address-normalisation step fails on roughly one run in thirty for a particular input. An engineer proposes a prompt fix, runs that input five times without seeing a failure, and marks the ticket resolved. The tech lead pushes back. What change to the verification would make the claim defensible?

options.A: Run the input enough times that seeing no failures would be unlikely under the original rate, and report the resulting confidence rather than a pass.
options.B: Run the input five times against both the old and the new prompt and compare the failure counts between the two arms directly.
options.C: Set temperature to zero for the verification run, so a single clean execution is sufficient to demonstrate the fix holds.
options.D: Add the input to the regression suite and rely on the nightly run to surface the failure over the following weeks if the proposed fix has not in fact resolved anything.

items.question: In a prompt library managed as versioned code, where should the few-shot examples used by a template live?

options.A: In a shared examples database queried at render time, so that improvements to an example propagate to every template using it at once.
options.B: Versioned in the same artefact as the template, because changing an example changes the prompt's behaviour.
options.C: In the eval suite only, referenced by the template at build time, so that examples and test cases can never drift apart from one another.
options.D: In a per-environment configuration file, so staging can be given richer examples than production without requiring a code change.

items.question: A healthcare software company wants a recurring signal on whether AI assistance is improving developer experience, to sit alongside its delivery metrics rather than replace them. Previous attempts produced a number that moved without anyone being able to explain why. Which survey design is most likely to produce a usable signal?

options.A: A single quarterly question asking each engineer to rate the assistant from one to ten, tracked as a trend line and reported to engineering leadership at the close of every quarter.
options.B: An open-text quarterly prompt inviting engineers to describe their experience, coded into themes afterwards by two members of the platform team.
options.C: A short, frequent survey about specific recent experiences — waiting time, confidence in unfamiliar code, friction in review — using identical items each cycle.
options.D: An annual anonymous survey covering all developer tooling, so the assistant can be compared against every other tool in one consistent instrument.

items.question: At 23:50 a bank's internal assistant for branch staff begins returning answers missing the mandatory regulatory disclaimer that a post-processing step is supposed to append. Branches are closed and the assistant is used only during branch hours, 08:00 to 18:00. A quality monitor paged the on-call engineer automatically. The likely cause is a change that shipped at 18:00; the deploy pipeline requires two approvers and the second approver is unreachable overnight. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Disable the assistant with its feature flag now, record the flag state and the monitor's evidence, and hand a full brief to the morning team.
options.B: Escalate to wake a second approver and revert the 18:00 deploy tonight, since a missing regulatory disclaimer is a compliance breach and cannot wait.
options.C: Leave the assistant enabled, set an alarm for 07:00, and reassess before branches open so that no action is taken on incomplete information.
options.D: Downgrade the page to a ticket for the owning team's business hours, since no user is affected while every branch is closed.

items.question: Why does an engineer's mental model of an AI-integrated service typically go stale faster than for a conventional service of similar size?

options.A: AI services tend to be written across more languages and runtimes, so knowledge decays as engineers move between the parts of the stack.
options.B: AI services carry more third-party dependencies than conventional services of the same size, and the resulting churn invalidates knowledge that was entirely accurate a quarter ago.
options.C: Behaviour depends on artefacts that move outside the code — prompts, retrieval corpora, model versions — so reading the code stops describing what the system does.
options.D: AI services are usually newer, so they have accumulated fewer conventions and less documentation than the older services surrounding them.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's platform team owns 34 feature flags across its AI features. Nineteen have sat at 100% for over six months. During an incident last quarter the team discovered that one kill switch no longer disabled anything, because the code path it guarded had been refactored away months earlier and nobody noticed. Which TWO practices address the underlying problem? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Rename every flag to include its creation date, so that stale flags are visible at a glance whenever anyone opens the management console.
options.B: Require a second approver for any production flag change, so that no flag is flipped or removed without another engineer reviewing the intent.
options.C: Give every flag an owner and an expiry date, and treat a flag past its expiry as a defect to be either removed or renewed deliberately.
options.D: Move all 34 flags into deployment configuration so they are versioned alongside the code that reads them and cannot drift from it.
options.E: Exercise each kill switch on a schedule in a production-like environment and assert that the guarded behaviour actually stops when it is flipped.

items.question: A grocery wholesaler parses emailed purchase orders with Claude and writes the result into its ERP. Overnight, 12% of orders begin landing in the ERP's exception queue with a "quantity field invalid" error. The AI team's dashboards show normal parse success, normal token counts and normal latency. The ERP team reports no change on their side, and neither team has deployed in a week. Both teams are on the bridge. What is the most productive framing for the next fifteen minutes?

options.A: Treat this as an ERP validation change until that team can prove otherwise, since the rejection message originates inside their system and only they can interpret it.
options.B: Compare the quantity values the AI service emitted overnight against those it emitted last week, since a shift in output shape satisfies both teams' dashboards.
options.C: Have the AI team roll back to the previous release and watch the exception rate, since that isolates which side of the boundary is responsible fastest.
options.D: Ask the ERP team to relax the quantity validation temporarily so orders keep flowing while the two teams investigate the cause properly.

items.question: A pharmaceutical analytics group is onboarding six engineers onto its Claude-based literature-screening service. Leadership wants them experimenting freely from week one, but is nervous: another group's runaway evaluation loop consumed a large unbudgeted amount overnight last quarter. Which setup best serves both concerns?

options.A: Give each engineer a personal key on a sandbox account with a hard spend cap and no production data access, and let them raise their own cap up to a limit.
options.B: Issue the shared team key to all six and require the tech lead to approve in advance any run expected to exceed a defined token budget.
options.C: Restrict experimentation to a locally hosted small open model, and grant provider access only once an engineer has shipped their first reviewed change.
options.D: Grant production key access from day one and rely on the existing monthly spend alert plus a review requirement on any newly added call site.

items.question: At 14:00 an insurer discovers that a prompt change deployed at 09:00 has been generating policy summaries stating an incorrect excess amount. In those five hours, 2,300 summaries were generated and written to customer policy records; roughly 400 of those were also emailed to customers. Reverting the prompt is a ten-minute deploy. Beyond the revert, what should the response plan be?

options.A: Regenerate all 2,300 summaries with the corrected prompt and overwrite the stored records in place, so every policy file is immediately accurate again.
options.B: Notify the 400 customers who were emailed, and leave the remaining 1,900 stored summaries as they are, since no customer has seen those.
options.C: Quarantine all 2,300 records so none can be served or re-sent, then regenerate them while preserving the originals as evidence of what was issued.
options.D: Raise a data-quality ticket so the 2,300 records are corrected by the nightly batch job that already reconciles policy documentation.

items.question: Engineers at a telco routinely paste production log excerpts into an AI assistant to debug faster. A security review finds those excerpts have included subscriber identifiers and, on two occasions, a database connection string. A blanket ban was announced last year and quietly stopped being observed within a month. Which TWO measures are most likely to reduce exposure while keeping the workflow? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Require every engineer to complete annual training on what may and may not be shared with external tools, with a signed acknowledgement.
options.B: Provide a one-command log-fetch tool that strips subscriber identifiers and credential patterns before the excerpt ever reaches the clipboard.
options.C: Shorten production log retention so that far fewer sensitive excerpts exist for anyone to copy in the first place.
options.D: Route assistant traffic through a monitored egress proxy that blocks any request containing a credential pattern and records the attempt.
options.E: Restrict production log access to the current on-call engineer, so at most one person at a time is in a position to copy an excerpt.

items.question: A council's benefits-advice chatbot handles about 4,000 sessions a week. Complaints arrive days later through a separate case-management system, describing what the bot said but carrying no identifier that exists anywhere in the AI platform's telemetry. Investigators currently search by approximate time of day and remembered phrases, and succeed maybe half the time. What should the team change?

options.A: Log the full conversation transcript for every session, so that free-text search across the logs becomes reliable enough to find any complained-about exchange.
options.B: Add a question to the complaint form asking for the date and approximate time of the session, so investigators can narrow the search window considerably.
options.C: Index the bot's response text in a search engine so an investigator can paste a quoted phrase from the complaint and retrieve the matching session.
options.D: Show a short session reference in the chat interface and require it on the complaint form, so the case record carries the key that resolves to the trace.

items.question: A retailer's platform team surveys its 90 engineers and reports that AI assistance saves each of them about 4 hours a week. A finance partner converts 360 saved hours a week into roughly 9 full-time equivalents and circulates the figure as an annualised saving. Over the same six months, delivery output is flat, headcount is unchanged, and no team has taken on additional scope. The engineering director is asked to endorse the number. What is the accurate characterisation?

options.A: Time saved on a task is not capacity realised; unless freed hours were redirected into identifiable work, the saving is notional and the flat output is the evidence.
options.B: The saving is real but lagging; delivery metrics typically take two to three quarters to reflect a capacity increase of this magnitude in a team of this size.
options.C: The estimate is conservative, since it counts only authoring time and omits the time saved on code review, incident response and onboarding new joiners.
options.D: The calculation should be redone using fully loaded cost rather than base salary, which would make the annualised saving materially larger than stated.

items.question: A university admissions platform's Claude-based document-completeness checker scores 96% on a 500-case eval set assembled from historical applications. In the first week of the intake period, admissions staff report it misses genuinely missing documents in roughly one application in eight. The team re-runs the eval suite against the currently deployed prompt and still gets 96%. What is the most useful next step?

options.A: Move the checker to a higher model tier, since production inputs are evidently harder than the historical cases the eval set was built from.
options.B: Add the reported production failures to the eval set and re-run the suite, so that it reflects the reality admissions staff are experiencing during this intake week.
options.C: Lower the confidence threshold at which the checker flags an application as incomplete, trading a rise in false positives for fewer missed documents.
options.D: Sample the failing production applications and compare their composition against the eval set's, since the two figures can only diverge if the populations differ.

items.question: Which observation most reliably distinguishes an AI-feature quality incident from an infrastructure incident affecting the same feature?

options.A: Quality incidents begin gradually as behaviour drifts, whereas infrastructure incidents start abruptly at an identifiable moment in time.
options.B: In a quality incident the health signals stay green, because the feature is responding successfully with content that happens to be wrong.
options.C: Quality incidents affect a subset of users with particular inputs, whereas infrastructure incidents affect everyone using the feature at once.
options.D: Quality incidents are reported by users, whereas infrastructure incidents are caught by monitoring before any user has noticed anything.

items.question: Which artefact should not be committed into a prompt library repository?

options.A: The output schema each template is expected to produce, expressed as a schema file the consuming service also validates against.
options.B: The golden eval cases used to grade each template automatically on every pull request that touches it.
options.C: Real customer transcripts captured from production and pasted in verbatim to serve as few-shot examples.
options.D: A changelog describing behavioural changes between template versions for the benefit of downstream consumers.

items.question: A logistics operator is writing the first-five-minutes checklist that will be attached to every page for any of its AI features. The design goal is that a responder with no prior context can decide within five minutes whether to contain, and what containing would actually mean. Which THREE items must the checklist put in front of them? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Which flags and kill switches govern this feature, their current state, and precisely what behaviour each one stops.
options.B: A full architecture diagram of the feature covering every tool, dependency and downstream consumer in the chain.
options.C: What changed recently across all four behaviour-bearing surfaces: code, prompt version, retrieval corpus and resolved model version.
options.D: Where this feature's output is persisted or forwarded, so the responder knows what remains live after generation stops.
options.E: The feature's monthly cost and its per-request cost trend over the preceding thirty days, for context on its business importance.

items.question: A commercial insurer is rolling out Claude-drafted responses to broker enquiries. Enquiries range from routine questions about cover limits to complex claims-history queries where a wrong statement can create a coverage dispute the insurer must honour. The delivery team's default plan is a random 5/25/100 percentage rollout on all enquiry types at once. The head of underwriting objects. What rollout design better fits this risk profile?

options.A: Roll out by enquiry category, beginning with the lowest-consequence categories and admitting harder ones only as each clears its own quality gate.
options.B: Keep the random percentage rollout but require an underwriter to review every drafted response until the feature reaches full exposure at 100%.
options.C: Keep the random percentage rollout and suppress any draft where the model's stated confidence falls below a threshold tuned during the 5% stage.
options.D: Roll out by broker account, beginning with the smallest brokers by premium volume and expanding upward in account size over four weeks.

items.question: A team samples traces at a low baseline rate for cost reasons, but support needs to capture a complete trace for one specific user while that user is still on the phone. Which mechanism provides this?

options.A: Temporarily raise the global sampling rate to 100% for the duration of the support call, then return it to the baseline afterwards.
options.B: Replay the user's most recent request through a debug endpoint configured to capture everything, and investigate the replayed trace.
options.C: A sampling override set for that session at the edge and propagated downstream, forcing every service to retain its spans.
options.D: Extend span retention for the affected service so the user's earlier traces remain available for a longer investigation window.

items.question: A defence-logistics contractor must be able to replay a completed agent run for post-hoc review — the entire trajectory, not a single call — and demonstrate to an auditor that the replay reflects what happened. Which THREE things must be captured for each step? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The full message list as it stood at the start of that step, including any compaction or truncation the runtime applied before sending.
options.B: The exact tool invocation arguments the model produced and the exact results that were returned into the conversation.
options.C: The wall-clock duration of each step, so that the replay can reproduce the original pacing of the run.
options.D: A human-readable narrative summarising the agent's reasoning at each step, written when the run completed.
options.E: The resolved model version and the tool definitions in force at that step, since both can change between the run and the replay.

items.question: An organisation wants two headline metrics for AI-assisted engineering that are hard to inflate through behaviour change alone. Which TWO qualify? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Lines of code accepted from the assistant per engineer per week, aggregated to team level for reporting.
options.B: Number of assistant sessions started per engineer per week, as a measure of how embedded the tool has become.
options.C: Change failure rate: the proportion of deployments that require a hotfix, rollback or forward fix.
options.D: Proportion of pull request descriptions that mention the assistant was used in producing the change.
options.E: Defect escape rate: the proportion of defects found in production rather than before release.

items.question: A commodities trading firm runs an agentic research assistant. Median run cost is modest, but the most expensive 1% of runs cost around 60 times the median, because the agent iterates through many tool calls before terminating. Monthly spend is dominated by that tail, and per-desk budgets are being breached by a handful of runs each month rather than by general usage. Which control addresses this most directly?

options.A: Lower each desk's monthly budget so that the existing tail is absorbed within a smaller ceiling and overruns become visible sooner.
options.B: Enforce a per-run token and step budget, with the agent required to return its best partial result when the budget is reached.
options.C: Move the assistant to a cheaper model tier so that every run, tail runs included, costs proportionally less than it does today.
options.D: Alert the desk head whenever a single run exceeds ten times the median cost, so unusually expensive runs get reviewed after the fact.

items.question: A prompt library ships inside the application artefact. A production prompt defect needs correcting sooner than the normal release train allows. What is the appropriate practice?

options.A: Maintain a runtime override store for emergencies, so that any prompt can be replaced without a deploy whenever speed matters more than process.
options.B: Accept the release train's cadence, since bypassing it is what produced the drift problem that keeping prompts in the artefact was meant to solve.
options.C: Move the prompt permanently out of the artefact and serve it from configuration, so that hot fixes are always available for this template in future.
options.D: Use the expedited release path the codebase already has for hot fixes, so the prompt change is still reviewed, versioned and rolled back as one artefact.

items.question: Within twenty minutes, three unrelated AI features at a logistics platform — route summarisation, customer-email drafting and invoice extraction — all begin producing noticeably worse output. The three are owned by different teams, run on different services, and use entirely different prompts. Error rates, latency and throughput are normal everywhere. What should the incident commander direct first?

options.A: Enumerate what the three features share — gateway, model alias, embedding index, redaction middleware — and check each for a change inside that window.
options.B: Have each owning team investigate its own feature in parallel and report back within thirty minutes, since three teams can cover far more ground than one.
options.C: Declare a provider-side incident, since simultaneous degradation across unrelated services is characteristic of a change in the underlying model.
options.D: Roll back the most recent deploy on each of the three services, on the basis that a shared release train may have carried a common library change.

items.question: A run team at a national rail operator is taking ownership of a Claude-based delay-explanation service from the team that built it. Handover completes in two weeks. The run team is experienced at operating conventional services but has never owned an AI system, and the building team is being reassigned immediately afterwards. In the first handover session the run team asks what to concentrate on. What should they establish first?

options.A: A complete walkthrough of every prompt template in the service and the reasoning behind each instruction it contains.
options.B: Which signals tell them the output has gone bad, and which control stops it — ahead of anything about how the internals work.
options.C: A cost model for the service so they can forecast and defend their operating budget across the first year of ownership.
options.D: Access to the building team's on-call rota for three months, so anything they cannot resolve can be escalated to the original authors.
